claims.claim: conventional top-1/top-2 MoE with 8–16 experts suffers knowledge hybridity and knowledge redundancy
split each expert into m by shrinking intermediate dim to 1/m, activate mK; C(16,2)=120 vs C(64,8)=4,426,165,368
Ks shared experts always active, routed activations reduced by Ks; prototype credited to DeepSpeed-MoE
2B alpha1=0.01 no device loss; 16B alpha1=0.001 (higher hurts, no efficiency gain); 145B alpha1=0.003 alpha2=0.05 over 4 devices
first layer kept dense because load balance converges especially slower
2B: Pile loss GShard 1.867 vs DeepSeekMoE 1.808; TriviaQA 10.2 vs 16.6
1/2/4 shared experts Pile loss 1.808/1.806/1.811; ratio 1:3 adopted
disabling shared expert (+1 routed) Pile loss 1.808→2.414

finer granularity not used at 16B due to computational efficiency of too small experts

hindsight_claims.claim: Qwen3-MoE excludes shared experts unlike Qwen2.5-MoE; uses global-batch load balancing loss
Kimi K2: 384 experts, 1 shared, 1 dense layer, no expert grouping; higher sparsity brings infrastructure complexity
DeepSeek-V4 replaces initial dense FFN layers with hash-routed MoE layers
Keep Routing crucial for MoE RL stability since V3-0324
Llama 4 Maverick: alternating dense/MoE layers, 128 routed + 1 shared, each token to one routed expert

boundaries: All comparisons retrain baselines on DeepSeek's own corpus; 40% is a training-FLOPs ratio, not latency
Dense×16 upper bound is a constructed 16-shared-expert model
Multiple-choice weakness attribution is the authors' hypothesis based on an unpublished internal study
Expert-specialization evidence is indirect (loss sensitivity), not interpretability
